Pandita Ramabai
PUN-dit-uh RAH-muh-bye
proper noun
Pandita, a Sanskrit honorific for a learned woman, “scholar”; Ramabai, joining the divine name Rama with the respectful bai, “lady.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922) was an Indian woman of high learning, born to a Brahmin scholar who broke custom by teaching his daughter the Sanskrit scriptures. Orphaned young and widowed early, she rose to rare renown as a Sanskrit teacher, granted the title Pandita for her mastery. Yet the systems she had studied gave her no answer to the misery of India’s child-widows and abandoned women, and her searching led her to Christ, in whom she found the living God the idols could not give. She was baptised in 1883 and ever after confessed Jesus as Saviour and Lord. Settling near Pune, she founded the Mukti Mission, a refuge that in time sheltered thousands of widows, orphans, and famine victims, where they were fed, taught a trade, and above all told of the Saviour. She translated the whole Bible into Marathi from the original tongues, that her people might read the Scriptures plainly. A revival of prayer and confession swept Mukti in 1905. Ramabai never softened the gospel to suit her culture; she named the bondage of caste and idolatry and held up Christ as the only deliverer. Her life joined rigorous learning, fierce compassion, and a settled faith in the God who hears the cry of the helpless.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An Indian Brahmin scholar converted to Christ who founded the Mukti Mission for widows and orphans and translated the Bible into Marathi.

expand to see more

PANDITA RAMABAI, an Indian Christian scholar and reformer (1858–1922).

Born to a Brahmin family and granted the title Pandita for her Sanskrit learning.

Converted to Christ and baptised in 1883 after the idols gave her no hope.

Founded the Mukti Mission near Pune, a refuge for widows, orphans, and the famine-stricken.

Translated the whole Bible into Marathi from the original languages.

📖 Key Scripture

Jas 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

Psa 146:9 — "The LORD preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow:"

Joh 8:36 — "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed."

Isa 1:17 — "Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Her unflinching naming of idolatry and caste as bondage rebukes the modern habit of treating false religions as parallel paths to God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Ramabai is that pure and undefiled religion cares for the widow and the fatherless and confesses Christ as the only Saviour. She did not blend her old learning with the gospel; she renounced the idols that had failed her and clung to the Son who makes free indeed.

Her Mukti Mission joined mercy to truth, sheltering the helpless body while preaching the saving word. Against every claim that all faiths lead alike to God, her life testifies that she found in Christ what the systems of men could never supply, and spent herself that others might find Him too.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

A Sanskrit honorific for a learned woman joined to a respectful Indian name.

expand to see more

Pandita Ramabai — Pandita, “learned woman, scholar”; bai, “lady.”

The title Pandita was conferred for her public mastery of the Sanskrit scriptures.

Mukti, the name of her mission, means “salvation” or “deliverance.”

Her Marathi Bible was rendered directly from the Hebrew and Greek.

A revival of confession and prayer broke out at Mukti in 1905.

Usage

"Pandita Ramabai turned her rare learning to the service of India’s forsaken widows."

"The idols had no answer for Pandita Ramabai, but Christ set her free."

"Thousands of orphans found bread and the gospel at the Mukti Mission of Pandita Ramabai."
